newsitem.title: NORWAY: FEATURE - Natural gas and bacteria -- a gourmet delight?.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Natural gas and bacteria -- a gourmet delight?.

text.p: What do you get if you mix natural gas with bacteria, add a little oxygen, ammonia and water, and flavour with a few minerals?
Maybe not a gastronomic delight, but a highly rich protein source called bioprotein. Now used to enrich animal feeds, it could soon be included in the human diet.

"We think the human market is enormous, both in nutritional terms and hydrolysates (taste additives)," said Jon Huslid, president of Norferm, a joint venture between Statoil, Norway's state-owned oil company, and Norwegian pharmaceuticals group Nycomed ASA.
Stavanger-based Statoil is the dominant player in Norway's thriving offshore sector.
The two companies are building a plant to produce an annual 10,000 tonnes of bioprotein -- reddish-brown granules created through a chemical process -- using natural gas held deep in the seabed.
"If you buy a packet of dried chicken soup it's not real chicken, the tastes are man-made from protein. In the future the taste may well come from bioprotein," Huslid told Reuters.

European Union countries consume around one million tonnes of protein for animal/fish feed each year and about 600,000 tonnes, derived primarily from soya beans and milk for human consumption such as in bakery products and sausages.

The plant, the first of its kind in the world, will be built at Tjeldbergodden on the west coast in mid-Norway, near to a methanol plant where gas from the Heidrun field in the Norwegian Sea is used as feedstock.
Some of that gas will be diverted to the bioprotein plant when it begins production in mid-1998.
NATURAL GAS MAKES PROCESS CHEAPER

Similar processes using methanol as feedstock were developed in the 1960s and 1970s, but were found to be too costly. By using natural gas directly from the seabed, Norferm's process is much cheaper and cost effective.
"To produce one kilogram of bioprotein using natural gas is three to four times cheaper than using methanol," Huslid said.
"The resulting protein is excellent for growth and has a very high nutritional content. It is easily converted into energy and therefore growth," he said.

Bioprotein is a protein-rich biomass based on microorganisms, which use natural gas as the sole carbon and energy source. Oxygen, ammonia and minerals are also added to the process, which takes place in a closed reactor.
The new technology was developed over 10 years, beginning in 1985 by Dansk Bioprotein in the Danish town of Odense, more commonly known as the home town of fairytale writer Hans Christian Andersen.

Nycomed became a shareholder in Dansk Bioprotein in 1987 and Statoil acquired an interest in 1990. Four years later, Nycomed and Statoil set up Norferm, a 50/50 joint venture which now owns 98 percent of the Danish group.
The biomass culture consists of two groups of bacteria, spherical methanotrophic and rod-shaped heterotrophic, which are about one thousandth of a millimetre in diameter.

Natural gas is made up of a series of hydrocarbons -- molecules containing carbon and hydrogen only -- with the simplest hydrocarbon, methane accounting for about 90 percent, together with around five percent of ethane, two percent of propane and other higher hydrocarbons.

Methanotrophic bacteria use methane for growth. The methane is oxidised by the bacteria to biomass and carbon dioxide. Methanol, formaldehyde and formic acid are produced in the process as metabolic intermediates.

Heterotrophic bacteria feed off the metabolites, the products of the chemical changes, from the methanotrophic bacteria. The main function of the heterotrophic bacteria is to use up oxidation products produced by their methanotrophic counterparts and the organic materials released into the fermentation broth where the reaction takes place.
HARVESTING CAN START AFTER A FEW DAYS
Four types of bacteria are placed into a loop-type fermentor, along with the other ingredients. The bacteria consume the feedstocks and multiply every two to three hours.

By careful control of the feedstock gases, an equilibrium is reached for optimium production of biomass and harvesting can start after just a few days. The bacteria are capable of producing over one kilogram of protein per two cubic metres of gas in the fermentor every hour.

Once harvested from the system, the bacteria are heated to 130 degrees Celsius during which they "explode" like popcorn to release reddish-brown granules. These granules contain 70 percent protein, 12 percent carbohydrates, 10 percent fat and eight percent minerals.
The Danish Ministry of Agriculture approved natural gas bioprotein as an animal/fish feed additive in 1993, and the EU followed in mid-1995.

Norferm now has applied to the authorities in Britain, Denmark and Norway to approve the bioprotein for human consumption as taste additives in processed foods such as dried soups, sauces and spices and in snacks.
